title: Bar model for word problems
examples: When should I use a bar model?
Is there a difference between part-whole and comparison?
Can I use a bar model for multiplication?

explain.say: Today we will learn to use bar models for word problems. Bar models help us see the math picture.
First we look at part-whole models. These show a total and the parts that make it up. For example, if you have 10 apples total, and 4 are red and 6 are green, the whole is 10. The parts are 4 and 6.
Next we look at comparison bars. These compare two different amounts. For example, if John has 12 stickers and Mary has 8 stickers, the total is not needed. We just compare 12 and 8.
Let us try a problem. If a class has 20 students, and 12 are girls, we use a part-whole model. The total is 20, and one part is 12. The other part is 20 minus 12, which is 8.

faq.q: What is the difference between part-whole and comparison?
faq.a: In a part-whole model, you know the total and some parts. In a comparison model, you are just finding the difference between two separate amounts.

faq.q: Do I always need to draw a model?
faq.a: Drawing a model helps you organize your thinking. It is a great way to check if you understand the problem before solving it with numbers.

faq.q: If I find the total, should I use part-whole?
faq.a: Yes, if the problem tells you that the parts add up to a whole amount, the part-whole model is perfect for you.
asks: When should I find the total?
Does knowing the total mean part-whole?

faq.q: Can I use bar models for finding the difference?
faq.a: Yes, finding the difference is comparing two amounts. You use the comparison bar model to show how much bigger or smaller one amount is than the other.
asks: Is 'how many more' a comparison bar?
Do I use comparison for difference?

faq.q: What if the problem is about groups of things?
faq.a: If the problem is about groups, you might need to draw several small bars to represent each group. Think about what the total represents.
asks: What if there are many groups?
Does 'groups of' mean a bar model?

facts: A part-whole model shows a total and the parts that make it.
A comparison model shows two separate amounts to compare them.
If you know the total and one part, you find the missing part by subtracting.
Finding the difference between two numbers is a comparison problem.

quiz.say: A baker made 30 cookies. He sold 15 cookies in the morning and 10 cookies in the afternoon. Which model shows the total of 30, with parts 15 and 10?

options.show: A model showing a whole of 30, divided into two parts of 15 and 10.
options.say: A model showing a whole of 30, divided into two parts of 15 and 10.

quiz.why: This is a part-whole model because the two parts (15 and 10) add up to the total (30).

wrong.0: This model only shows the two parts and forgets the total amount of 30.
wrong.1: This model only subtracts the afternoon sales and ignores the morning sales.
wrong.3: This model only shows one subtraction, forgetting the 10 cookies sold later.

quiz.say: A farmer planted 40 seeds. He planted 22 seeds in the north field and the rest in the south field. What model shows this situation?

options.show: A part-whole model with a total of 40, and two parts of 22 and 18.
options.say: A part-whole model with a total of 40, and two parts of 22 and 18.

quiz.why: The seeds in the north and south add up to the total seeds planted, making it a part-whole model.

wrong.0: This only shows the two parts and forgets the overall total of 40 seeds planted.
wrong.2: This ignores the fact that the 22 seeds are only part of the total 40.
wrong.3: This only shows the final subtraction step, not the structure of the total and its parts.
